newsitem.title: TAIWAN: HK handover swells Taiwan independence mood - poll.
newsitem.headline: HK handover swells Taiwan independence mood - poll.

text.p: Pro-independence sentiment rose in Taiwan after Hong Kong's absorption by Beijing, with most people rejecting union with rival China under an autonomy scheme pioneered in the new region, a poll reported on Friday.

If given only two choices -- reunion with the communist mainland or full independence from China -- a record 43 percent of 949 respondents interviewed by the United Daily News said they would opt for independence.
The poll, conducted on July 1-2 after the British colony became a Special Administrative Region of China, showed that 34 percent of respondents supported union with mainland China.
The newspaper noted that it was the first time that support for independence had outstripped support for reunification in its regular polling, which dates to 1989.
In the first poll conducted in November 1989, 55 percent said they wanted to reunify with the mainland, compared with only six percent who supported independence, it said.
The most recent poll, in January, indicated 34 percent wanted independence, while 37 percent preferred reunification.

When given the additional choice of "maintaining the status quo", 43 percent said they wanted to see things stay unchanged -- with capitalist, democratic Taiwan in the hands of the Nationalist Republic of China and the mainland with the communist People's Republic.
Many people maintain that the status quo is de facto independence.
Asked about their personal identity, more than half said they regarded themselves as Taiwanese, while 30 percent identified themselves as Chinese.
Beijing, which has seen Taiwan as a renegade province since a 1949 civil war split, threatens to attack if the island drops its official pro-unification stance and pursues independence.
Beijing maintains that Hong Kong's return and that of Portuguese-run Macau in 1999 will leave Taiwan as the only territory awaiting "reunification with the motherland".
Beijing is pressing Taiwan to accept union under a "one country, two systems" model being implemented in Hong Kong, saying Taiwan could keep its political system and army.
Taipei, which embraces multi-party democracy, officially espouses union but only when all of China is under a free, democratic system -- a scheme Taiwan calls "one country, one good system".
The poll showed almost 50 percent of Taiwan people felt indifferent about Hong Kong's shift to mainland sovereignty.
Some 25 percent said they were glad to see the handover, while 13 percent said they were saddened by it.
Sixty-two percent said they would not accept "one country, two systems", compared with 21 percent who said they would.

President Lee Teng-hui on Thursday assailed Beijing for trying to force Taiwan to accept communist China's sovereignty, saying national unification can spring only from democracy, freedom and equitable prosperity.
